conclusion_template: For an m x n matrix A, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n. The rank equals the dimension of the column space (image), and the nullity equals the dimension of the null space (kernel). This is a consequence of the dimension theorem for linear maps.
reasoning_framework: The rank-nullity theorem is the fundamental dimension-counting identity in linear algebra. Given a linear map T: V -> W represented by matrix A, the domain V decomposes as a direct sum of ker(T) and a complement isomorphic to im(T). Thus dim(V) = dim(ker(T)) + dim(im(T)), which translates to n = nullity(A) + rank(A). This holds for all matrices regardless of whether they are square. Computational verification: compute RREF, count pivot columns (= rank), count free columns (= nullity), confirm they sum to n.
primary_authority: Axelrod & Hausmann, Linear Algebra Done Right

conclusion_template: Eigenvalues lambda satisfy det(A - lambda*I) = 0. For an n x n matrix, there are at most n eigenvalues (counting multiplicity). The sum of eigenvalues equals the trace; the product equals the determinant. Real symmetric matrices have all real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
reasoning_framework: The characteristic polynomial p(lambda) = det(A - lambda*I) is a degree-n polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues. By Vieta's formulas, the sum of roots = -coefficient of lambda^(n-1) = trace(A), and the product of roots = (-1)^n * constant term = det(A). The Spectral Theorem guarantees that real symmetric matrices are orthogonally diagonalizable: A = Q*D*Q^T where Q is orthogonal and D is diagonal with real eigenvalues. For non-symmetric matrices, eigenvalues may be complex. Algebraic multiplicity >= geometric multiplicity for each eigenvalue.
primary_authority: Strang, Linear Algebra and Its Applications

conclusion_template: LU decomposition factors A = LU (or PA = LU with pivoting) where L is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal and U is upper triangular. It enables efficient solving of multiple systems Ax = b by forward/back substitution in O(n^2) per solve after an O(n^3) factorization.
reasoning_framework: Gaussian elimination without row swaps directly produces L and U: the multipliers used to zero entries below pivots form L, and the resulting upper-triangular matrix is U. Partial pivoting (PA = LU) swaps rows to use the largest available pivot, improving numerical stability. Doolittle's method computes L with unit diagonal; Crout's method puts the diagonal in L instead. Solving Ax = b becomes: solve Ly = Pb by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back substitution. Each substitution is O(n^2), making LU efficient for repeated solves with different b vectors. LU exists for all nonsingular matrices (with pivoting).

conclusion_template: QR decomposition factors A = QR where Q has orthonormal columns and R is upper triangular. It is computed via Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, Householder reflections, or Givens rotations. QR is the basis of the QR algorithm for eigenvalue computation and is numerically superior to normal equations for least squares.
reasoning_framework: Classical Gram-Schmidt applies orthogonal projection to each column of A, subtracting components along previously computed orthonormal vectors. Modified Gram-Schmidt recomputes projections against partially orthogonalized vectors for better numerical stability. Householder QR uses reflections to zero below-diagonal entries column by column, achieving backward stability. For least squares Ax ~ b, the QR approach solves Rx = Q^T*b, avoiding the condition-number-squaring problem of normal equations (A^T*A). The QR algorithm for eigenvalues repeatedly factors A_k = Q_k*R_k and forms A_{k+1} = R_k*Q_k, converging to Schur form.

conclusion_template: The SVD factors any m x n matrix A = U * Sigma * V^T where U (m x m) and V (n x n) are orthogonal, and Sigma is diagonal with non-negative singular values. SVD reveals the rank (number of nonzero singular values), provides the best low-rank approximation (Eckart-Young theorem), and defines the pseudoinverse.
reasoning_framework: Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of A^T*A (or A*A^T). The columns of V are eigenvectors of A^T*A; columns of U are eigenvectors of A*A^T. The condition number cond(A) = sigma_max / sigma_min. The pseudoinverse A^+ = V * Sigma^+ * U^T where Sigma^+ inverts nonzero singular values. For least squares, x = A^+ * b is the minimum-norm least squares solution. The best rank-k approximation keeps only the k largest singular values (Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem). SVD is the most informative decomposition but costs O(mn * min(m,n)).
primary_authority: Strang, Linear Algebra and Its Applications

conclusion_template: For a symmetric positive-definite matrix A, the Cholesky decomposition A = LL^T exists uniquely, where L is lower triangular with positive diagonal entries. It costs half the operations of LU and is numerically very stable without pivoting.
reasoning_framework: Positive definiteness means x^T*A*x > 0 for all nonzero x, which ensures all eigenvalues are positive and all leading principal minors are positive. The algorithm computes L column by column: l_jj = sqrt(a_jj - sum(l_jk^2, k<j)), and l_ij = (a_ij - sum(l_ik*l_jk, k<j)) / l_jj for i > j. The operation count is n^3/6, half that of LU (n^3/3). Cholesky is the method of choice for solving normal equations A^T*A*x = A^T*b since A^T*A is always positive semidefinite (positive definite when A has full column rank). It also tests positive definiteness: if Cholesky fails, the matrix is not positive definite.
primary_authority: Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms

conclusion_template: The determinant det(A) is multiplicative: det(AB) = det(A)*det(B). Row swaps flip the sign; scaling a row by c multiplies det by c; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged. det(A) = 0 iff A is singular. For triangular matrices, det is the product of diagonal entries.
reasoning_framework: The determinant encodes the signed volume scaling of the linear map represented by A. Cofactor expansion along row i: det(A) = sum_j (-1)^(i+j) * a_ij * M_ij where M_ij is the (i,j) minor. This recursive formula costs O(n!) for an n x n matrix but is exact. For practical computation, row reduction to triangular form gives det in O(n^3): track sign changes from row swaps and multiply the diagonal. Key identities: det(A^T) = det(A), det(cA) = c^n * det(A), det(A^{-1}) = 1/det(A). Cramer's rule uses determinants to express solutions but is computationally impractical for large systems.

conclusion_template: The least squares solution to Ax ~ b minimizes ||Ax - b||^2 and satisfies the normal equations A^T*A*x = A^T*b. When A has full column rank, the unique solution is x = (A^T*A)^{-1} * A^T*b. For numerical stability, QR or SVD methods are preferred over forming the normal equations directly.
reasoning_framework: Geometrically, the least squares solution projects b onto the column space of A. The residual r = b - Ax is orthogonal to col(A), giving A^T*r = 0, hence A^T*(b - Ax) = 0, which yields the normal equations. Forming A^T*A squares the condition number (cond(A^T*A) = cond(A)^2), which can cause numerical issues. The QR approach: factor A = QR, then x = R^{-1}*Q^T*b, preserving the original condition number. SVD gives the minimum-norm solution via the pseudoinverse. Applications include polynomial fitting (Vandermonde matrix), linear regression, curve fitting, and signal processing.
primary_authority: Bjorck, Numerical Methods for Least Squares Problems

conclusion_template: Gram-Schmidt takes a linearly independent set {v1,...,vk} and produces an orthogonal (or orthonormal) set {u1,...,uk} spanning the same subspace. Classical Gram-Schmidt can lose orthogonality due to floating-point errors; modified Gram-Schmidt is more stable.
reasoning_framework: The algorithm iteratively removes the component of each new vector along previously computed orthogonal vectors: u_k = v_k - sum(proj_{u_j}(v_k), j<k). Normalizing each u_k gives an orthonormal basis. In exact arithmetic, classical and modified GS produce identical results. In floating-point, classical GS can catastrophically lose orthogonality when vectors are nearly dependent, while modified GS recomputes projections against partially orthogonalized vectors. Twice-iterated classical GS matches modified GS in stability. Gram-Schmidt directly produces the QR factorization: Q columns are the orthonormal vectors, R entries are the projection coefficients and norms.

conclusion_template: The inverse of a nonsingular n x n matrix A is computed by augmenting [A | I] and reducing to [I | A^{-1}] via Gauss-Jordan elimination. A is invertible iff det(A) != 0 iff rank(A) = n iff its columns are linearly independent.
reasoning_framework: Gauss-Jordan elimination applies row operations to transform the left half of [A | I] to I; the same operations transform the right half from I to A^{-1}. Partial pivoting ensures numerical stability. The computation costs O(n^3) operations. Equivalent characterizations of invertibility: (1) det(A) != 0, (2) rank = n, (3) null space is trivial, (4) A has n pivots, (5) eigenvalues are all nonzero, (6) 0 is not a singular value. For solving Ax = b, computing A^{-1} explicitly is less efficient and less stable than LU factorization; use inverse only when needed for multiple right-hand sides or analytic expressions.
primary_authority: Meyer, Matrix Analysis and Applied Linear Algebra

conclusion_template: A basis for a vector space V is a linearly independent set that spans V. All bases have the same cardinality, which defines dim(V). For R^n, the standard basis has n vectors. Key subspaces of a matrix: column space (rank), row space (rank), null space (nullity), left null space.
reasoning_framework: A set {v1,...,vk} is linearly independent iff the only solution to c1*v1 + ... + ck*vk = 0 is c1 = ... = ck = 0. It spans V iff every vector in V is a linear combination of the set. A basis satisfies both conditions; it is a minimal spanning set and a maximal independent set. The Steinitz exchange lemma proves all bases have equal size. For an m x n matrix A, four fundamental subspaces: col(A) in R^m (dim = r), null(A) in R^n (dim = n-r), row(A) in R^n (dim = r), left null(A) in R^m (dim = m-r), where r = rank(A). These subspaces satisfy: col(A) perp left_null(A) and row(A) perp null(A).

conclusion_template: Every linear transformation T: R^n -> R^m is represented by a unique m x n matrix A such that T(x) = Ax. T is injective iff ker(T) = {0} iff nullity = 0; surjective iff im(T) = R^m iff rank = m; bijective iff both (requires m = n and det != 0). Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication.
reasoning_framework: A function T is linear iff T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v) for all scalars a,b and vectors u,v. The matrix representation A has columns A*e_j = T(e_j). The kernel (null space) ker(T) = {x : T(x) = 0} is a subspace of the domain; the image (range) im(T) = {T(x) : x in domain} is a subspace of the codomain. Rank-nullity: dim(ker) + dim(im) = dim(domain). Change of basis: if B and C are bases for domain and codomain, then [T]_{B,C} = C^{-1} * A * B. Similar matrices represent the same transformation in different bases: B = P^{-1}*A*P.

conclusion_template: Matrix norms measure matrix 'size': Frobenius norm = sqrt(sum of squares), spectral norm = largest singular value, 1-norm = max column sum, infinity-norm = max row sum. The condition number cond(A) = ||A|| * ||A^{-1}|| measures sensitivity of Ax = b to perturbations. cond >> 1 indicates ill-conditioning.
reasoning_framework: A matrix norm || || is submultiplicative: ||AB|| <= ||A||*||B||. Induced norms satisfy ||Ax|| <= ||A||*||x||. The condition number bounds relative output error: ||delta_x|| / ||x|| <= cond(A) * ||delta_b|| / ||b||. For the spectral norm, cond_2(A) = sigma_max / sigma_min. Rule of thumb: if cond ~ 10^k, you lose about k digits of accuracy in solving Ax = b. Ill-conditioning arises from near-linear-dependence of columns (near-singular matrix). Preconditioning transforms the system to reduce condition number before solving.
primary_authority: Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms

conclusion_template: Gaussian elimination reduces a matrix to row echelon form (REF) or reduced row echelon form (RREF) via three row operations: swap, scale, add multiple. Partial pivoting selects the largest-magnitude entry in each column as pivot, ensuring numerical stability. RREF is unique for any matrix.
reasoning_framework: Forward elimination zeros entries below each pivot to produce REF (upper triangular for square matrices). Back substitution or continued elimination to RREF makes each pivot = 1 and zeros entries above pivots. Without pivoting, small pivots amplify rounding errors. Partial pivoting (swap rows to maximize |pivot|) bounds the growth factor, ensuring stability in practice. Complete pivoting (swap both rows and columns) gives even better stability but is rarely needed. The RREF of a matrix is unique and reveals: rank (number of pivots), pivot variables vs free variables, null space basis, and solution set structure for Ax = b.

conclusion_template: A real symmetric matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable: A = Q*D*Q^T where Q is orthogonal (Q^T = Q^{-1}) and D = diag(lambda_1,...,lambda_n). A general matrix is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently iff geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity for every eigenvalue.
reasoning_framework: The Spectral Theorem guarantees that real symmetric matrices have (1) all real eigenvalues and (2) a complete set of orthonormal eigenvectors. This makes A = Q*D*Q^T with Q orthogonal. For non-symmetric matrices, diagonalizability is not guaranteed. A is diagonalizable iff its minimal polynomial has no repeated roots. Defective matrices (geometric < algebraic multiplicity for some eigenvalue) require Jordan normal form instead. Applications of diagonalization: computing matrix powers (A^k = Q*D^k*Q^T), matrix exponentials, solving linear ODEs, and principal component analysis.
primary_authority: Strang, Linear Algebra and Its Applications

conclusion_template: Matrix multiplication is associative ((AB)C = A(BC)), distributive over addition (A(B+C) = AB+AC), but generally NOT commutative (AB != BA). The product of m x n and n x p matrices yields m x p. Multiplication cost is O(mnp) for naive algorithm.
reasoning_framework: Entry (i,j) of AB = sum_k a_{ik} * b_{kj}, which is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Non-commutativity means AB and BA may differ in value or even in dimensions. Special cases where AB = BA: A and B are diagonal, or A and B are polynomials in the same matrix, or one is a scalar multiple of I. Block multiplication partitions matrices into submatrices and multiplies as if blocks were scalars (when dimensions are compatible). Strassen's algorithm achieves O(n^{2.807}) for square matrices; theoretically optimal exponent is unknown but < 2.372.
primary_authority: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms
